root.note: skholḗ first meant spare time, then what people did with it: discussion and study, and the place for that.

history: School comes from a word for free time, which may surprise anyone who has sat in a classroom. Greek skholḗ meant leisure, and then what educated people did with their leisure: talk, read and learn. Aristotle set it against both rest and work. Latin borrowed it as schola, and it spread with Roman schools across Europe. Spanish added an e- at the start, as it did to many words with s + consonant, and short o became ue, as in suelo. In Spain you meet it daily in autoescuela and escuela de idiomas. The same word gave French école, Italian scuola, English school and German Schule.
historyEinfach: Escuela comes from a Greek word. Its first meaning was ‘free time’! Rich Greek people used free time to talk and learn. So the word came to mean ‘a place to learn’. Latin took the word, and it went all over Europe: English school, German Schule, French école. In Spain, you learn to drive at an autoescuela.

elsewhere.text: English school is from the same Latin word, so the leisure idea is hiding there too.
French shares the e- at the start with Spanish.
In the Basque Country you will also hear ikastola, a modern coinage: ikasi ‘to learn’ + ola ‘little house’, for schools taught in Basque.
